content:
If you are new to the UK and have persistent joint pain or swelling, ask a GP for an assessment. In England, GP registration is free and does not require ID or proof of immigration status.

Who this guide is for

This guide is for refugees, people seeking asylum, newly arrived migrants and anyone who finds it difficult to navigate UK arthritis services. You can use it whether you already have an arthritis diagnosis or are seeking help for persistent joint symptoms.

What is arthritis?

Arthritis describes several conditions affecting joints. Osteoarthritis can cause pain and stiffness with movement. Inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis may cause persistent swelling, warmth, fatigue and prolonged morning stiffness. The right treatment depends on the diagnosis. Not every painful joint is arthritis.

Symptoms and when to seek help

Book a GP appointment if joint pain, stiffness or swelling persists, limits daily activities or repeatedly returns. Prompt assessment is especially important for persistent joint swelling or prolonged morning stiffness. A suddenly hot, very painful swollen joint, particularly with fever, needs urgent assessment to exclude infection. Seek emergency help for serious new neurological symptoms or life-threatening illness.

How to register with a GP

In England, registering with an NHS GP is free. You do not need ID, proof of address or proof of immigration status to register. If you do not have a fixed address, ask the practice about registering using an alternative contact address. Procedures across the UK nations vary, so check local NHS guidance. Ask the receptionist for an interpreter and give your preferred language and dialect.

GPs, physiotherapists and rheumatologists

A GP can assess symptoms, discuss medicines and decide whether tests or referral are needed. A physiotherapist may help with tailored movement, strength, function and confidence. A rheumatologist diagnoses and treats inflammatory arthritis and may prescribe disease-modifying medicines. Bring your current medicine list, previous results and questions to appointments.

NHS eligibility and healthcare costs

Entitlement to free secondary care and prescription-cost support depends on the UK nation, immigration circumstances and service type. Refugees and asylum seekers may qualify for exemptions, but individual circumstances matter. Do not assume all care is free or that care is unavailable. Seek advice from NHS staff or an accredited migrant-support organisation and consult current official guidance.

Everyday exercise and pain management

Start with gentle mobility, short walks and comfortable sit-to-stand movements from a stable chair. Build up gradually according to symptoms and function. Heat may help stiffness; a wrapped cold pack may ease short-term swelling. Protect skin from burns or cold injury. Pacing activities, sleep routines and medication reviews can help. Avoid exercising through severe pain or a hot, swollen joint.

Housing, income and mental wellbeing

Small or temporary accommodation can make movement, rest and medication storage difficult. Ask your housing contact, GP or support worker about accessible facilities, safe heating, occupational therapy and local support. Persistent pain can affect mood and sleep; ask your GP about psychological support. Do not stop prescribed medicines without advice because of cost or fasting.

Arthritis and faith

People who pray while kneeling or standing may need comfortable adjustments such as a stable chair. A trusted religious adviser can help with religious questions. Before Ramadan or other fasting periods, discuss medicines, food requirements, hydration and dosing times with your pharmacist or prescriber. Do not change prescribed treatment independently.

For women, older adults and people at work

Pregnancy planning and some arthritis medicines require specialist review. Menopause, caring duties and work demands can also affect symptoms and access to care. Older adults who live alone may benefit from strength and balance exercises, falls assessments and home adaptations. Working adults can ask employers about reasonable adjustments and official support schemes where eligible.

Language and interpretation

Ask NHS services for a professional interpreter and specify the language and dialect. For medical discussions, avoid relying on children to interpret.
